Brunt

BRUNT -- origin uncertain, perhaps Old Norse for a fiery charge; think of taking the main blow of an attack. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Brunt is the worst or heaviest part of something.

Coastal villages bore the brunt of the hurricane while inland towns saw only rain.

Worked Example

When the company's plan fails, the executives who designed it stay comfortable upstairs -- but the warehouse workers lose their overtime, their bonuses, and finally their jobs.

Those workers are absorbing the worst part of the failure -- its main blow. That heaviest share of damage or hardship is exactly what the brunt is, as in 'bear the brunt of the layoffs.'

How Strong Is It? — impact → brunt → burden

impact vs. brunt

impact vs. brunt: Impact is more neutral than brunt -- every collision has an impact, while the brunt is specifically the worst, heaviest share of it that someone or something absorbs.

burden vs. brunt

burden vs. brunt: Burden lasts longer than brunt: a burden is a heavy load carried over time, while the brunt is the concentrated main blow of a particular event.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — brunt

root — brunt: a sharp blow; the shock of an attack (Middle English (origin uncertain, possibly Old Norse bruna, 'to charge forward like fire'))

Put it together

Put it together: Brunt appeared in Middle English meaning a sharp blow or the shock of an attack; its deeper origin is uncertain -- possibly Old Norse bruna, 'to charge forward like fire' -- and it left no other common English relatives, standing alone much like the attack-words onslaught and assault it often keeps company with.

Use the root in a new word: onslaught

Use the root in a new word: onslaught: The goalkeeper somehow held firm against the final ten-minute onslaught.
